strengths: Introduces a novel timestamp-free framework for video temporal localization that uses structural tokens <ent> and <tst> to partition videos into event and transition segments, avoiding the limitations of numeric timestamp generation in video LLMs.

Proposes query-focused captioning (QFC) to inject fine-grained event semantics into structural token representations; ablations support its effectiveness and show boundary-centric methods cannot leverage QFC in the same way.

Extensive zero-shot evaluations on E.T.Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights across grounding, dense captioning, and complex reasoning tasks show strong and consistent gains over boundary-centric and general video LLMs, including larger baselines.

Controlled experiments replacing boundary-centric localization modules in TimeChat, VTGLLM, and E.T.Chat with MeCo demonstrate generality and isolate the benefit of the proposed structural token grounding.

The paper is well written, with clear motivation, informative figures, and sufficient implementation details in the supplementary material, including hyperparameters, prompt templates, and QFC generation pipeline.

The results provide compelling evidence that semantic-driven temporal localization with LLMs can outperform timestamp-centric approaches, which is a meaningful direction for video-language understanding.
weaknesses: The inference procedure for MeCo is under-specified in the main text: Algorithm 1 assumes structural token embeddings are already available and does not show how QFC tokens and structural token sequences are generated at test time, nor how their hidden states are extracted.

Equation (3) appears to contain summation/indexing errors (the outer and inner sums both use t, and the inner limits are t_i^e to t_i^e rather than t_i^s to t_i^e), which should be corrected and clarified to ensure technical soundness.

The ablation study in Table 5 is somewhat ambiguous and does not cleanly isolate the effects of <tst> and QFC; some metrics do not improve consistently when adding QFC, making the claimed synergy harder to verify.

Despite strong overall gains, Charades-STA R@1_0.7 is not better than E.T.Chat/TRACE, and the threshold-based multi-segment retrieval and highlight scoring may partly favor semantic-similarity methods, requiring more analysis of failure cases and threshold sensitivity.

Query-focused captions are generated using ground-truth event timestamps during training and external captioning/GPT summarization models, introducing potential biases and unanalyzed inference-time caption quality/cost; robustness and quality of QFC at test time are not thoroughly evaluated.

Reproducibility is limited by reliance on external/proprietary models and the absence of released code or checkpoints; the computational overhead and scalability of QFC generation are also not analyzed.

The claim of being the first video LLM-based timestamp-free temporal localization framework is strong and would benefit from more careful qualification and positioning relative to prior semantic/segmentation-based localization approaches.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel timestamp-free temporal localization framework that replaces boundary timestamp generation with structural tokens and contrastive grounding, which is a fresh direction for video LLMs.

The empirical results are strong and consistent across E.T.Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights, with substantial improvements over boundary-centric baselines, especially in grounding and complex reasoning tasks.

The controlled replacement experiments in Tables 4 and 6 provide useful evidence that the proposed structural-token approach can improve multiple base architectures, and the ablation studies examine the contributions of transition tokens and query-focused captioning.
The method is evaluated on a broad suite of temporal localization tasks, including grounding, dense captioning, and grounded video QA, demonstrating generality across task types.
The paper is generally well written and clearly motivated, with informative figures and a coherent narrative around semantic-driven localization.
weaknesses: A critical inference detail is missing: Algorithm 1 assumes that the set of structural token embeddings (and thus the number of segments M') is known, but the manuscript does not explain how the LLM decides how many event/transition tokens to generate at inference. Without this, the method is not reproducible and its practical validity is unclear.

Equation (3) contains serious technical/typographical errors: the summation indices appear incorrect, and the denominator is written as t_i^e - t_i^e, which would be zero. This makes the central structural token grounding loss mathematically ill-defined as presented.

The 'timestamp-free' claim is somewhat overstated: ground-truth event boundaries are still required during training to construct structural token sequences and to extract clips for query-focused caption generation. The method avoids generating timestamps at inference, but it does not eliminate reliance on timestamp supervision.

Query-focused captions are generated using external models (MiniCPM-V-2.6 and GPT-4o-mini), but the paper provides no analysis of caption quality, hallucination, or how errors in generated captions affect localization. This pipeline also introduces reproducibility and dependency concerns.

The zero-shot evaluation protocol is not fully convincing. E.T.Instruct may include training data from Charades-STA/QVHighlights, and it is unclear whether the reported Charades-STA and QVHighlights results are truly zero-shot. For multi-segment QVHighlights, the thresholding strategy is not adequately specified or validated, raising concerns about tuned thresholds or test-time hyperparameter selection.

The ablation results weaken the claim that both transition tokens and query-focused captioning are necessary. With QFC, adding <tst> improves F1gnd only from 40.4 to 40.6, while <tst> without QFC is much stronger; the interaction is not deeply analyzed.
On Charades-STA, MeCo does not consistently beat E.T.Chat on the stricter R@1_0.7 metric, and the paper downplays this by calling it 'on par' rather than analyzing the drop.
The paper lacks a limitations section and does not provide enough error analysis or failure cases for a method that depends on generated captions and threshold-based segmentation.
There is no discussion of ethical or bias considerations for the generated captions and localization outputs, which is relevant given the use of proprietary captioning/summarization models.

strengths: Introduces a novel timestamp-free framework, MeCo, that replaces boundary timestamp generation with structural tokens and contrastive grounding, directly leveraging video LLMs' semantic and temporal-structure understanding.
The query-focused captioning task is a well-motivated and effective addition that bridges fine-grained event semantics with localization, and the ablations show it contributes meaningfully.

Extensive experiments across E.T.Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights demonstrate consistent and often large improvements over boundary-centric temporal localization video LLMs, including on complex reasoning tasks.
Controlled comparisons that plug MeCo into existing architectures (TimeChat/VTGLLM) and the ablation studies provide useful evidence that the gains are not solely due to model scale or training data.
The paper is generally clear, well-organized, and includes implementation details and prompt templates in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Equation (3) contains apparent notation/typographical errors: the summation indices and denominator (t_i^e - t_i^e) are invalid, which harms technical clarity and reproducibility.

The zero-shot claim on Charades-STA and QVHighlights is potentially overstated if E.T.Instruct includes training splits from these datasets; the paper should explicitly clarify data leakage/exclusion.
The construction of transition segments is underspecified. It is unclear how neighboring transition segments are defined or segmented during training, and how sensitive performance is to this choice.

For QVHighlights multi-segment retrieval, the thresholding strategy for converting semantic similarities to event segments is not fully described, including threshold selection and sensitivity analysis.
Query-focused captions are generated by external models (MiniCPM-V-2.6 and GPT-4o-mini); the paper does not analyze caption quality, hallucination, or the impact of caption noise on localization.

Some tables have duplicated or inconsistent rows (e.g., Table 1), and the highlight detection comparison may favor MeCo because it directly uses continuous similarity scores while baselines generate discrete timestamps; this should be discussed more carefully.

strengths: Presents a novel semantic-oriented framework for video temporal localization that avoids autoregressive boundary timestamp generation and instead leverages video LLM semantic understanding through structural tokens and query-focused captions.

The method is technically coherent: it combines generative supervised fine-tuning (structural token generation and query-focused captioning) with a contrastive structural token grounding module, and the ablation studies validate key design choices such as the <tst> token, QFC, and loss variants.

Extensive experiments across E.T. Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights demonstrate strong empirical gains on many grounding, dense captioning, and highlight detection metrics, often outperforming boundary-centric video LLM baselines and even specialist models in fine-tuning settings.
Reproducibility is well supported with detailed appendices, hyperparameter settings, pseudo-code, prompt templates, data synthesis description, and annotated code/data in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: The reporting in Table 1 is partially inconsistent or unclear: MeCo rows show '-' for SFT Data, Epochs, and LoRA even though the method is fine-tuned on E.T.Instruct, making controlled comparison with baselines harder to interpret. The claim of consistent outperformance is also not fully supported, e.g., MeCo (ETChat 3.8B) is worse than E.T.Chat on GVQ.

Query-focused captions are generated by external models (MiniCPM-V-2.6 and GPT-4o-mini) without human validation or quality analysis, which introduces potential label noise, hidden bias, and additional reproducibility/cost concerns.

The novelty is somewhat incremental: structural tokens and contrastive grounding resemble prior timestamp-token and boundary-matching approaches. The method still relies on ground-truth event boundaries to construct training labels, so the 'timestamp-free' framing applies to inference rather than the whole pipeline.

There are apparent technical/presentation issues: Eq. (4) seems to contain incorrect summation bounds and undefined notation (e.g., t_i^c), which may hinder understanding and reproduction. Some inference details around overlapping events and softmax normalization also need clearer exposition.

Boundary precision is not consistently improved, with fine-grained metrics such as R@1_0.7 sometimes trailing boundary-centric baselines. The paper acknowledges this trade-off, but a deeper analysis and mitigation would strengthen the contribution.

strengths: Proposes a novel timestamp-free semantic-oriented framework for video temporal localization using structural tokens and query-focused captions, which is a refreshing departure from boundary timestamp generation.
Extensive experiments on E.T. Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights demonstrate strong performance, often outperforming timestamp-centric methods.
Ablation studies validate the contributions of structural tokens, query-focused captioning, and the contrastive grounding loss.
The paper provides code and generated data in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The query-focused captioning (QFC) training data is generated from ground-truth event timestamps, which leaks privileged information. At inference, the model must generate QFC without ground-truth boundaries, creating a significant train-test mismatch and potentially inflating results.

The 'zero-shot' evaluation on Charades-STA and QVHighlights is questionable because E.T.Instruct may contain training data from these benchmarks, and MeCo is fine-tuned on E.T.Instruct. The paper does not sufficiently clarify the overlap.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently fair: many baselines use different base LLMs, larger training data, and different numbers of epochs. The self-implemented fine-tuning comparisons are limited to a few models.

The structural token grounding loss does not enforce temporal continuity, so frame-to-token assignment can yield fragmented or non-contiguous segments. The paper acknowledges failure cases but lacks a principled solution.
Claims of 'consistently outperforming' timestamp-centric methods are overstated: on several metrics (e.g., EPM, DVC F1, SLC, GVQ), MeCo is not the best or gains are marginal.
The paper has presentation issues, including unclear table entries (MeCo rows show '-' for SFT Data, Epochs, LoRA), typos, and insufficient details on QFC generation and inference robustness.

Novelty is incremental: structural tokens and contrastive grounding resemble existing token-based temporal grounding and chain-of-thought approaches; the core idea may not be sufficiently distinct for a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper proposes a novel semantic-oriented framework, MeCo, that avoids boundary timestamp generation by using structural tokens (<ent>/<tst>) and query-focused captions, better exploiting the semantic understanding of video LLMs for temporal localization.

The technical design is clear and cohesive: structural token generation captures holistic video temporal structure, query-focused captioning provides fine-grained event semantics, and contrastive structural token grounding maps token hidden states to frames for localization.

Extensive experiments across E.T. Bench, Charades-STA, and QVHighlights cover grounding, dense video captioning, complex reasoning, and highlight detection, showing strong zero-shot and dataset-wise fine-tuning gains over timestamp-centric and specialist baselines.

Ablation studies validate key components, including the <tst> token, query-focused captioning, the asymmetric grounding loss, and comparisons with boundary-centric strategies and simple CLIP/EVA thresholding baselines.

The paper includes a reproducibility statement, detailed implementation and training details, pseudo-code for inference, and provides code/data in supplementary material; results also show scalability from 3.8B to 7B models.
Significant improvements are demonstrated on several metrics, especially QVHighlights mAP/HIT@1 and temporal video grounding F1, suggesting the approach is practically effective.
weaknesses: The claims of being “timestamp-free” and “consistently outperforming” are somewhat overstated: training still relies on ground-truth boundary timestamps for structural token labels and query-focused caption extraction, and inference still computes frame-level probabilities to derive timestamps. In addition, MeCo (3.8B) underperforms E.T.Chat on GVQ (0.6 vs. 3.7), so not every task improves.

Query-focused captions are generated by an external captioning model and summarized by GPT-4o-mini, which introduces potential noise and external-model dependency; the paper lacks human evaluation or sensitivity analysis of caption quality.

The structural token grounding loss is asymmetric and uses softmax over all frames, which may limit fine-grained boundary precision; the paper acknowledges lower R@1_0.7 performance, and dataset-wise fine-tuning still trails specialist models on the strictest grounding threshold.

Evaluation comparisons are somewhat uneven: baselines use different base LLMs, training data sizes, and numbers of epochs, and the grayed-out non-zero-shot cells complicate direct comparison. Although self-implemented E.T.Instruct comparisons help, some fairness concerns remain.
Qualitative failure-case analysis is limited and largely illustrative; multi-event and overlapping-event handling is described but not quantitatively evaluated in depth.

There are minor presentation issues, such as likely typos/formatting problems in equations and table references, and no discussion of inference cost/latency despite the additional projectors and contrastive grounding.
